concept.tagline: True multi-core shared-memory Python parallelism in CPython 3.13t+ (PEP 703) using Biased Reference Counting and per-object critical sections.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of free-threaded Python (PEP 703)—from why the GIL existed to Biased Reference Counting, C-extension `Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED` traps, and thread-safe state.

spark.summary: Free-threaded Python (PEP 703, CPython 3.13t+) removes the Global Interpreter Lock so multiple threads execute Python bytecode simultaneously across CPU cores within a single shared memory space.
spark.keyTakeaway: CPU-bound Python threads can now scale across cores without multiprocessing pickle overhead, provided C-extensions declare Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED and shared mutable state is synchronized.

**Core Mechanics:** CPython's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) existed because `Py_INCREF`/`Py_DECREF` reference counting was not thread-safe.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Free-Threaded CPython Import & GIL Fallback States (GIL DISABLED -> CRITICAL SECTION -> GIL RE-ENABLED); 8-Core Free-Threaded Workers Over Shared 2 GB Rule Graph (ThreadPool (8) -> threading.local() -> 2 GB Rule Graph -> mimalloc + BRC).

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore bypassing the GIL for CPU workloads, false sharing, and asyncio.

learningJourney.title: What is Free-Threaded Python (PEP 703)
learningJourney.explanation:
CPython's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) existed because `Py_INCREF`/`Py_DECREF` reference counting was not thread-safe. **PEP 703** (`python3.13t`+) removes the GIL by introducing **Biased Reference Counting (BRC)**, `mimalloc` per-thread heaps, immortal objects (PEP 683 for `None`/`True`/small ints), and per-object **critical sections** for `list`/`dict`/`set`.

Multiple OS threads can now execute Python bytecode simultaneously across CPU cores inside one shared heap.

learningJourney.title: Why we need No-GIL (and why Compound Races Now Surface)
learningJourney.explanation: Previously, CPU-bound Python required `multiprocessing`, duplicating multi-gigabyte model weights or rule graphs across N processes and serializing payloads over IPC pipes. Under `python3.13t`, shared-memory threads eliminate that duplication—but code like `counter += 1` or `d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1`, which accidentally relied on GIL bytecode-switch atomicity, now exhibits real **lost-update data races**.

ideas.title: Assert `not sys._is_gil_enabled()` at Startup
ideas.description: Run CI with `PYTHON_GIL=0` and check `sys._is_gil_enabled() is False` in startup health probes so legacy wheels never silently serialize your cluster.

ideas.title: Avoid False Sharing on Shared Counters
ideas.description: Accumulate metrics in `threading.local()` and merge periodically instead of bouncing cache lines on one global counter.

learningJourney.explanation: Free-threaded Python fills the CPU + shared-memory gap between `asyncio` (high-concurrency I/O) and `multiprocessing` (process isolation).

costs: OS thread scheduling and stack virtual memory waste RAM on idle sockets.

benefits: Multi-core CPU scaling with zero-copy shared heap.

benefits: Strong process isolation and works with any legacy C extension.
costs: Duplicates N copies of large memory structures and pays pickle IPC cost.

benefits: Lowest memory per task (~KB) for 10k+ I/O connections.
costs: Single core only for Python CPU execution.

beginner.byteSummary:
**The Core Idea (Beginner):** CPython's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) existed because `Py_INCREF`/`Py_DECREF` reference counting was not thread-safe.

**How It Flows:** Think of Python GIL-Free Concurrency, Asyncio & Coroutines as a clear step-by-step chain: GIL DISABLED -> CRITICAL SECTION -> GIL RE-ENABLED -> ThreadPool (8) -> threading.local().

**Why Beginners Should Care:** CPU-bound Python threads can now scale across cores without multiprocessing pickle overhead, provided C-extensions declare Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED and shared mutable state is synchronized.
